utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. The Chamber decided that it would start this morning in the absence of the witness because we ended up yesterday two parties fighting about what the document would be or would not be, or what it would demonstrate or not demonstrate. Now, Gotovina Defence apparently knows the document. Ms. Mahindaratne it as well. The witness authored it, apparently. So he knows -- so everyone knows and the battle starts and the Chamber has no idea yet what we are talking about. So we do it in a different way. Let's have these documents on the screen and then, Ms. Mahindaratne, you can tell us, first of all, what the document is. We can look at the date, we can look at the time-frame, we can look at whatever. And then tell us briefly what you expect the witness could tell us about and what your views on the document are. Then if Mr. Kehoe disagrees, then he will certainly be on his feet and tell you that you're totally wrong, and then finally we'll know what the issues are and then we can ask the witness about the issues because he, apparently as the author, knows best. Could we get these documents we had yesterday, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That would be 65 ter 7320, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And ... Which is a document presented in an English version, five pages. It is a -- the first page being a letter sent by the witness to the Republic of Croatia state attorney's office in Zagreb, in which he says that he attaches to this letter the requested data for the district state attorney office in Zadar, the municipal state attorney's office in Zadar, and the municipal state attorney's office in Benkovac. That is dated the 30th of August, 2006. That's --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may also draw Court's attention to the subject heading; that is, "Documentation Regarding the Criminal Acts in the Storm," it reads.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. "Documentation Regarding the Criminal Acts in the Storm." I take it -- I'll also have a look at the original. So at least a major difference with the other documents we saw is that they were all contemporaneous and this is a document created only relatively recently.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That's correct Mr. President. Apart from which, Mr. President, this document contains details --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll further go to the -- any further comments to be made in relation to the first page, Mr. Kehoe. Did we miss anything which might turn out to be relevant?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we move to the next page, and I would have a look at the originals to start with. Ms. Mahindaratne, what now is -- first of all, let's have a look at what the columns are.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If I could just state, Mr. President. This particular chart on page 2, which is only on page 2, is a list of charges filed against known perpetrators by the county state attorney's office in Zadar, and there are seven entries there. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me have a look. What we have, we have a -- it says chart 1. We have the -- how it was reported, name of the -- personal data of the suspect, description of the offence, place and date on which the offence allegedly was committed, whether there is any victim and injured person, what and when was decided in relation to this, and what finally the decision by the court has been. So these are the columns we have here. Now, Ms. Mahindaratne, you made a selection, apparently, to be translated. First of all, is there a -- the first page says the data you requested in relation to Storm. Now, is there any -- I noted yesterday that I think I saw that, at least some of the crimes were committed before Storm had started.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do we know -- is there any clue, have the parties any idea were these tables or these charts made at the time that the latter was created, or was it -- is there any agreement on that or not, because, otherwise, we'll ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think that I can -- this particular document was made after the fact, and it was after the change in jurisdiction. As the witness pointed out in his witness statement, there was in 1997 a change back in jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: He made these in -- excuse me, 2006, where --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So it was -- my simple question was, is there any agreement on when the chart was made, was that at the time the letter was created. Apparently 2006 is when the letter was created so the answer is, as far as you are concerned, Mr. Kehoe, that this document was created in 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's my understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That is my understanding, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apparently there seems to be no disagreement on that. Now, Ms. Mahindaratne, on what basis -- I mean, we see table 1, we see table 2, where the numbering starts again. Do we have any idea on the structure of this document? Every page starts a new numbering system.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. I could explain, actually, the structure if I'm given just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, your understanding of the structure.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yeah, as it is produced on the document, Mr. President, because when -- at the start of a new table there is a heading, and that's the basis on which we have translated. And if I'm allowed, Mr. President, I could just quickly take you through and it will be clear then to the Court and the parties how --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In order to avoid confusion, Ms. Mahindaratne is invited to explain to us how she understands the document. Whether that's a proper understanding, we'll hear from you, and finally we'll hear from the witness what it's all about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, Mr. President on that score, her understanding of the document is irrelevant, and I think should be put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but my problem is, Mr. Kehoe, and I hope you understand, that finally we'll find out what the witness can tell us about this document. The problem is that we start a battle already on matters where the Chamber has no clue whatsoever about what the issue is. So, we're at this moment, the only thing we're doing is trying to find out where there is an issue. For that purpose, Ms. Mahindaratne is invited --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- to explain to the Chamber, what, in her understanding, the document is about and how it is structured. Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And Mr. President if you go to page 3, that is the next page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 3 original or 3 in English?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: 3 original, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 3, I am on the third page in the original, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, that's the next page. Now, there, Mr. President that is a new chart, that is chart number 2 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: -- which is a list of charges filed against unknown perpetrators by the county state attorney's office in Zadar, and there are 14 entries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. Is that translated on page 3 of the English as well?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. -- it is translated on page 2 of the English. That is, the top chart, which is now on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When we are talking about page 2, are you referring to e-court pages or are you referring to --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: It's on the screen, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But I'm -- yes, sometimes I'm using, okay. That's page 3 in e-court, yes. List of charges against unknown perpetrators. And that corresponds, as you said, with the --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: With page 3 and 4 of the original version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 3 and 4 of the original.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: There are 14 entries, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's clear. So there we have a list of charges filed against unknown perpetrators. Then we continue, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. On page 5 of the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 5 of the original.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And we remain on the same page as the -- on the English version. There is a list of reported incidents to the county state attorney's office in Zadar. It says: "KTR," "KR" and "DO." There are two entries there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I move on, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And at page 6, chart number 4 starts, and that would be, Mr. Registrar, the next page on the English version. There is a translation. That's the top chart there, Mr. President, which is a list of reported incidents to the county state attorney's office and there -- I'm sorry. It's a list of charges filed against known perpetrators by the municipal state attorney's office in Zadar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And there are ten entries there. This is page 6 of the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There apparently are, yes. And then the next.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Next one starts at page seven of the original. We remain on the same page as the English translation, which is a list of charges filed against unknown perpetrators by the municipal state attorney's office in Zadar. There are 126 entries so this chart goes from page 7 to page 17 on the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So apparently the document tells us the charges brought by the -- by the various prosecutorial authorities against the known and unknown perpetrators, county and municipal, known and unknown.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President. There are also two more charts, if I could just point it out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And the sixth chart starts at page 18 of the original. And, Mr. Registrar, if could you move to the next page on the English translation. And that's a list of charges filed against known perpetrators --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the same for Benkovac, known and unknown.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. And there you have the sixth charge 277 entries going from page 18 to 35.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And then the last chart starts at page 36, which is against unknown perpetrators, 9 entries, and that is just one page there, the last page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do we agree until now what the document is about? That, at least, this is contained in the document, six portions. Is there any problem with the incomplete translation at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because it always lists the first and last one and we find in between, we find some matters perhaps we could not fully understand, such as the persons who reported sometimes. It seems to be an office rather than a person. But apart from that, and we have at least the word "indictment" and we have "judgement." We might not in every respect be fully capable of reading all of the document, but the structure seems to be clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I agree that the -- we have read what the document says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We do not agree on its completeness because this is an incomplete document which is why the Gotovina Defence did not use it, in that as the witness noted, his documents prosecuted by the Zadar county attorney was sent to Sibenik in 1997. When that was brought to our attention, the information in this document -- since it was not complete, we went back to the contemporaneous documents that we'd admitted into evidence. So ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So the question is, one of the issues may be why, in 2006, are there any documents produced which -- well, let's say do not give a complete picture, or do the other documents not give a complete picture? Ms. Mahindaratne, or is it overstated what we find in the contemporaneous documents? What's the issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, in the contemporaneous documents, the figures are mere statistics which are not supported; whereas in this table, if this table was properly examined, one sees that there are crimes which do not relate to crimes which are committed in relation to Operation Storm included as such. What the Prosecution wants to demonstrate to the Trial Chamber is that when this witness compiles data as -- and submits as prosecution's conducted by his office in relation to crimes committed in the aftermath of Operation Storm, he has included irrelevant cases, such as we saw yesterday, crimes relating to falsifying public document, crimes committed before operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What you say, the activities as presented in the statistical data are not presenting what they pretend to present, which, of course, what we then need to do -- to see whether there is any merit in such a statement, we have to go back to what data are gathered in the one document and what data are gathered in the other document. Now, from what I remember and all the other statistical data where the crimes were set out, I never saw any reference to forgery of documents. However, the total number was always split up in known offences; that is, 34, I think, it's -- well, so, therefore, then it would not only be including documents but also a kind of a falsification because they are attached to certain types of crimes. Whereas, you say in these, what we find here, we find different types of crimes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. President. And apart from that, even where the type of crime comes within the -- the nature of crimes that's relevant to the indictment, I would demonstrate that there are, for example, there are crimes that comes under Article 34, murder, which is listed here which in fact are killing incidents which is not within the scope of these proceedings, which are completely outside. For example --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How do we know that the factual data on which this report of 2006 is based, whether that is the same set of factual data which were used to produce the statistics in 1995, 1996, Ms. Mahindaratne? How do we know?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, firstly I wanted to in fact, you know, ask the witness that now this document demonstrate that he, in response to a request from the state attorney for data on crimes prosecuted in relation to Operation Storm, he has sent in 2006 a whole entire list, and if in 2006 his list which he claims to be prosecutions conducted of crimes relating to Operation Storm includes irrelevant data, it's an inference that Court could draw that the statistics provided in 1995, 1996, so on, in the absence of the underlying materials supporting such statistics cannot be taken on the face of it. It's not reliable. That is the point that the Prosecution wants to demonstrate to Court, because at the moment all the material that has been placed before the Trial Chamber is just mere statistics. There are no informations supporting such statistics as it has been done in this table. And we believe, Mr. President, that this is one of the reasons that this table was not in fact tendered into evidence, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is suggestion on bad intentions by the other party, that is to keep away from the Chamber certain information which may be relevant. Let's just say that the Prosecution considers it's relevant to present this material as well, without talking about how bad the intentions are of the other party. Maybe good, maybe bad.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I can actually -- I'd like to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber finally does not have to determine about the intentions of the parties, but to have them determine on the basis of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may respond -- [overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. One second, I don't know whether Ms. Mahindaratne has already finished. Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If I may just point out, Mr. President. What I wanted to mainly place before the Trial Chamber is that the Defence has not produced, or at least this witness has not produced, a table of this nature supporting the statistics he has provided in the reports, and in the absence of such information the Trial Chamber would not be able to evaluate the relevance or for that matter to figure out if the statistics given by him indeed are related to prosecutions of crimes which are relevant to the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may, that claim is simply outrageous, and I will say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, I invited Ms. Mahindaratne to refrain from qualifications of bad intentions. If you would say that you disagree --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I disagree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You disagree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Respectfully, and if I may add this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We have presented to this Chamber what this witness said is the most accurate contemporaneous assessment of statistics, which is the statistics from 1995 going into 1996. Now, what he will say if the Prosecution asks is: Are the documents that you reviewed in 2006 complete, and do they include the files that were shifted and part of the Sibenik district that you lost jurisdiction over in 1997.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So what he will tell us, you expect that the difference could be explained by the borders of jurisdiction had changed and that therefore the data collected at a later stage would not include all of the data, which were gathered in 1995/1996. Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if I may, judge --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: -- with regard to the other crimes that -- such as forgery, et cetera, if Your Honour looked at D1554 as an example, on the last page of that document, and I don't know if Your Honour wants to bring it up, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I think if you --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I can just tell Your Honour what those other items are that we didn't go through, there are items such as Article 161, which is a traffic accident as well as 156. There's forgery, which is 206. Article 196, theft of cultural artifacts, Article 344, a violation of the customs law. There are any numbers of those articles set forth in that last page of the exhibit that chronicles some of those items, which of course, the numbers Your Honours can look at pale in comparison to the theft and robbery and larceny charges that were detailed on the prior page. So it is not that this witness overlooked chronicling them, they certainly had very little relevance herein.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, we're now talking about municipal Benkovac, municipal Zadar, and county Zadar. Mr. Kehoe, the contemporaneous reports sent to Mr. Lovric mainly, they covered what exactly, the prosecutorial activities Zadar county and --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And district courts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- municipal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Municipal courts, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And municipal courts. Was Benkovac included?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: At that juncture, yes, it was, until 1997.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Benkovac was included. And the -- yes. Ms. Mahindaratne, this list you are now -- these tables, let me just try to find the total number of charges.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I could give the total number of charges Mr. President. It's, according to this table, it's 445 for all three offices.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Whereas in the old documents, we had -- because we had already in November 1995, 705. We have 987 in February 1996. And, therefore, what we mainly have to do is to explore to what extent we're talking about the same set of data. Because it would be -- well, to say so, it would be rather stupid to present or to create something in 2006, a couple of hundred, in order to apparently support or give further details, where, in an earlier stage, you already had a number of a thousand people indicted.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may, and perhaps I didn't make myself clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: The purpose of this exercise is not to compare that data with the date given in this table but to demonstrate to Court the -- the methodology adopted by this witness in compiling data as prosecutions conducted by his office and his municipal prosecutor's offices. I wanted to demonstrate, in fact, this table not only with regard to those two entries that we dealt with yesterday but there are several other entries included as prosecutions of crimes relating to Operation Storm, which it meant, in fact, they're not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But that's -- okay. You say the witness, when authoring this document, was imprecise in including documents -- indictments or at least cases not related to Storm. Now, whether or not a forgery is related to Storm, it depends, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. Apart from that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: -- based on our assessment, in fact, we have highlighted those entries which are not relevant to the indictment, or for that matter to Operation Storm, the figures come down by 50 per cent. That's what we want to demonstrate to Court, that in fact what may be seen as 100 prosecutions, once one goes through with the -- entry by entry, it transpired that in fact the numbers are much less, about 50 per cent of the reported numbers. So given that, it would be -- it's not safe to accept the testimony or the witness's mere statistics in the absence of underlying material supporting those figures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you say it's --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: For example, Mr. President if I could just have a minute. There are in fact crimes listed here as those relating to Operation Storm but in fact committed before Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see your point. You say that this document created in 2006 raises a lot of questions. Now, you say that -- let's put those questions to the witness, and, because the inference should be, in your view, that, when, in 2006 he created tables which raise so many questions, why, and how could we rely on what was created in 1995/1996, where we do not even have an opportunity to verify. Is that the issue?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's at least I see what, in your view, the issue is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And as we conduct this examination, the Prosecution should say that we say, the Prosecution, there's a 50 per cent reduction in statistics. Can you account for that 50 per cent reduction in statistics because those were crimes committed out of the Sibenik-Krajina area and thereby were engulfed in those particular statistics. Because Your Honour is 100 per cent correct. We're looking at a different set of statistics as that that which came up in 1995 and that which the Prosecutor wants to put in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, evidence for the unreliability of the work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- of the witness. That's it, Ms. Mahindaratne?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That's it, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not more, not less. Then ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber is delighted that it has the impression that it has got now an idea of what we're talking about, which is always good if a chamber also knows what we are talking about. Could the witness be brought into the courtroom. Ms. Mahindaratne, it might be that we -- that we take it step by step. For example, the first question being: What data were you requested to send; perhaps also ask why, in 2006 such data were asked. I might put a few questions to the witness first to start with, if you do not mind. I'm so delighted that I know what we're talking about --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Please, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- that I'd like to give it some follow-up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Galovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, our apologies that you had to wait for a while.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Galovic, I would first like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration that you gave at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Galovic, yesterday we saw document, and that's how we concluded yesterday, a document on the screen. Could we have it on the screen again. Can you see it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You sent this letter to the state attorney's office in 2006; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you remember what request you received exactly, in response to which you sent this letter and attachment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is difficult for me to remember because I sent a great many such reports. I can conclude from this document that I only wrote in one line a sentence to the effect that I am sending information on such and such crimes. When they sent letters from the ministry and the state attorney's office, and I'm quite sure that it was the state attorney's office general that sent on letters to lower level state attorney's offices, they rarely specified what exactly it was that they were after. They said that they were interested in crimes related to Storm and that was it. So what we could do was to look into the registers, find the relevant information, and include it in our letters. What I can tell you with certainty is that all the data included in such letter is correct. Now, what can be concluded or observed or gleaned from the data, in my view, not much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll take it step by step --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- if you would not mind. So you don't remember what exactly was requested when you sent this, and you say this was quite common, that the requests for information were not very specific. Is that -- okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, nevertheless, specific or not, you sent this set of data. Now, we looked at other documents, contemporaneous reports you sent at the time. We have seen quite a number of them. Looking at them, we see indictments brought after approximately half a year after Operation Storm already, a thousand; whereas, in this document, where the attachment covers apparently the prosecutorial activity of the county and municipal attorney's office in Zadar and the municipal state attorney's office in Benkovac, all together go, well, let's say, in the 400 approximately. Could you explain to us why we find in this document a number which is -- apart from further details, but overall is less than half of what we find in the other documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can, and quite simply. Knin is not included here because it was transferred under the jurisdiction of Sibenik, and Knin constituted or covered the highest number of such incidents. In other words, Sibenik, having got Knin under its jurisdiction now, continued keeping records in relation to Knin. If you included in this number the data related to Knin, you would arrive at the figure I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You say the territorial scope is different, which explains for a difference in the total numbers. Now, in the letter, it refers to criminal acts in Storm. In the data, we find several offences listed which allegedly had been committed prior to Operation Storm. Could you explain the apparent discrepancy between the title, the subject as mentioned in the letter, and the appearance of crimes which are -- or offences which were committed prior to Storm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is evidently an error. The error is either in the date of the commission of the crime or the error was committed by someone in the municipal state attorney's offices. One has to keep in mind the fact that the data was collected in a very short period of time, and due to the speed with which one had to proceed, errors could have inadvertently have been made, and that's the only explanation I can provide for it. Let me also add that this is largely due, also, to the fact that the request for data was highly imprecise. I am still not quite clear on what offences related to Storm actually means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. Ms. Mahindaratne, I indicated that I would put a few questions first. It's your witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, it's not your witness. But you are examining -- cross-examining the witness at this moment. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Galovic, when you compiled the statistics that were reported in the documents that were submitted yesterday, did you prepare a table such as this or some kind of work product which listed out the cases, specific cases, which supported your statistics?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no need for something of this sort. We extracted all the data from the registers, which are regularly kept. All the data is verifiable. You can check it today in the relevant registers. Tables were produced as well, not of this kind. It depended on what sort of information was requested. If you're asking me about what we looked at yesterday, I will tell you how it is that I interpret the data. From the data you showed me yesterday, one cannot glean much. You can see what sort of workload lay in the hands of prosecutor's offices. The register -- or the record I kept for the purposes of the ministry is much better, because the individual charged with these matters in ministry had originally come from a prosecutor's office, and he knew what sort of information is helpful for specific -- in situations. Let me illustrate this. If you have data according to months, then, in addition to the workload, you can also see what sort -- what type of criminality was most frequent, what sort of criminality had to be prevented the most, in this way you can also organise your work and know where to focus, what to focus on. Collecting data is only a mechanical process.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr Galovic, I'm just trying to find out the manner in which you compiled the statistics you reported. Now here we have a table, a chart, you have prepared based on which one can easily gather the numbers, figures. Now, yesterday you reported, you know, in different reports number of statistics. Now, surely in order to get those figures your office and your municipal prosecutor's offices would have gone through a process in extracting the information from the registers. Now, can you explain to us how exactly were the information extracted and where was it recorded? In what manner? That's what I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I answered this question already but I will repeat it. As you say yourself, we had the information in our registers and the information was simply copied from the registers. The clerks in the office did that job. I would tell them what the period of time sought is, and what type of crime ought to be extracted. The next stage is that the information is collated. The clerk makes another check of the accuracy of information, if necessary, and the information is forwarded.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you just said you, in fact, instructed the clerks about the -- what -- what -- let me just say exactly what you said. Extracted information on this. Now, you instructed them on the time. Now what time-frame did you tell -- instruct the clerks to -- to extract the information for? What was the given time-frame? Did you say, Give me the -- the statistics of crimes prosecuted for this specific time-frame? What was the time-frame?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, we have seen many reports with all of them their own time-frame. Sometimes one month, sometimes anything after Operation Storm. So, unless -- I mean, I'm asking myself -- I take it that if you are preparing for statistics on a specific month that you instruct to collect the data for that month.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well Mr. President, I will specify --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the other one sometime it was cumulative for a longer period of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now we'll take your first report, D1554.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And before I move off this document, Mr. President, may I tender this document into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President I have no objection of it in that -- excuse me -- actually, the Croatian going in, of course, is not a full translation. I don't know how Your Honour wants to handle that. But in theory, we have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think in view of the evidence given by this witness, if the parties could live with an incomplete translation, because it seems to me that what, in view of the evidence, seems to be relevant of this document, is sufficiently accessible for English-speaking persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, you convinced me, so we have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Same is true for the other Defence teams. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit P2568.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Registrar, if I could have D1554.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Galovic, first of all, let's look at your report compiled for October 1995. Now, the figures given in this report --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And if you could go, Mr. Registrar, to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If you take as an example, there's a record of criminal files being raised against 305 persons under Article 126. Now, this relates to what period? When you instructed your clerks what did you tell them? To give you statistics of crimes committed for which period?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The preamble specifies this. It relates to a month. I don't know which specific month it states here in the document. But this is what the document states in the preamble.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, when -- now, you today, in relation to the previous document, you said even today you don't understand what it means by crimes related to Operation Storm. Now, what type of crime did you --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, could you refer to where it says "related to Operation Storm."

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because the testimony yesterday was, rather, in terms of time --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President I'm referring to testimony today. The witness just said this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But that was about the 2006 documentation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I hadn't finished my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Please finish your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, when you compiled these statistics, did you have an understanding as to what type of crimes you were supposed to look at?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are we talking about 1995?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: In 1995 when you compiled these statistics, were you specifically focussing on a type of crime as those related to Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By all mean, yes. However, the primary criterion was the liberated territory; in other words, offences committed at the time in the liberated territory and the time-period being that one month, depending on which period was being queried. And all the offences which were -- to which the municipal courts in Benkovac, Knin, Donji Lapac, Gracac, and the municipal court in Zadar were put on notice of, these are the subject-matter jurisdiction courts. You see, the courts at the time had that subject-matter jurisdiction only for offences which carried a sentence of maximum of five years. But let me not tire you with this information. The criterion was the crimes committed in the liberated territory and falling under the jurisdiction of these courts. This was the request we received.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, in saying "crimes," going by this document, we can see you have focussed on crimes against property and crimes against persons. Did you instruct your subordinate officers to focus on the type of -- for example, if you say crimes against property -- crimes against persons, if it's a killing incident, that the victims should be -- should be members of the Serb population, or did you take on board killing incidents in relation to all persons in that area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have that information there. Murder is listed first. Criminal offences against life and limb. Every report started with that heading first.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Galovic --

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not focus on crimes against property.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, excuse me. The witness has got to complete the answer before he's being interrupted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: But the witness was not answering my question. That's why I tried to focus him to my question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I got the impression that you had put this question to him already yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And he didn't answer, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let's -- [overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, enough with the commentary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What Ms. Mahindaratne would like to know, apparently, is whether in reporting and presenting statistical data, whether any distinction was made as to the ethnicity of the victims. That appears to be the question. Could you answer that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, not. I don't understand the question. I said so yesterday. Of course, no attention was paid to that. Murder is murder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, irrespective of the ethnicity or the victim. And they were all reported and there was no distinction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Irrespective of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, in relation to the cases of theft that's reported, was there any distinction made as to what type of theft should be taken on board, should be considered in compiling the data, or were all crimes of theft prosecuted by your office and the municipal prosecutor's offices during the period taken on board?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, could I perhaps make the question a bit more precise. You said whether all crimes of theft were prosecuted. Were all crimes of theft that were reported prosecuted without any distinction?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. That was not my question. My question was, whether in providing the statistics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Do the statistics include all crimes of thefts which were prosecuted, without drawing a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, okay. Fine. Now I understand your question. In these statistics you presented in 1995, were all prosecutions for all crimes of theft included?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, if I could go back to the previous chart, Mr. Registrar - I did not note down the exhibit number - P2568. And if we could move to page 2, Mr. Registrar, of the -- the original version.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Galovic, I want to draw your attention to entry number 1 there. There is a killing incident reported there, in relation to one Milos Mrkic, who is the accused and the victim is reported as Sava Mrkic. Now we in fact -- now this is reported as a killing incident prosecuted by your office in relation to Operation Storm, and this report is in -- filed in 2006. Now, we examined the corresponding crime file, and in fact this is what we found --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could bring up document 7325.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: -- and there, there are the details of the accused in the first paragraph there. And the crime is reported in second paragraph, if I would read to you. "As 5th August 1995 at about 1800 hours in Karin Donji in a house where, from the Maslenica operation, he lived with his wife Sava, who was unable to move, after the Croatian military police forces having liberated" -- you know, it goes on "... he set off a hand grenade with the intention to kill himself and his wife Sava, who was lying on bed in spite of her attempts to dissuade him." Now, the killing incident you reported as a prosecution relating to Operation Storm there in that chart. It's a killing incident, it's an attempted suicide, and it's the husband killing the wife. Now, this is what I tried to ask you: In compiling your statistics, you said you did not differentiate, make a distinction on the basis of who the -- the victim was. So in the absence of underlying material supporting your statistics, the Trial Chamber would not be able to evaluate the relevance of those statistics to this indictment. Are you able to provide the Trial Chamber --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, I object to the commentary by counsel. If counsel has a question, that's fine. Commentary about she believes is irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President I can --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, you can't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There are two basic rules, the one being, Ms. Mahindaratne, that you do not include comments in your question. You may put a leading question in cross-examination, there's no problem with that. But you can't first give your comments. And the second basic rule, is that this Chamber decides on what can be done and what cannot be done and not be objected.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My apologies, Mr. President, to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Galovic, first let me suggest to you that in the absence of and the underlying material, your statistics cannot be evaluated as being relevant to this indictment. Now, are you able to?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, that is -- I object to the commentary.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. First let me just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, you're doing exactly the same as you did before.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And, well, at least Mr. Kehoe learned that the Chamber decides, so the second basic rule has now been observed. The first basic rule we expect you to observe in the question you'll put to the witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Galovic, are you able to provided material or information such as that you provided in your table here, that we've just gone through, to the Trial Chamber so that we can evaluate your statistics? Are you able to provide that material to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can provide you with all the material. All the material I have I can send to The Hague. I have done that several times already. I don't know what is in dispute. I don't know which are the materials or documents that are being challenged. In connection with this case, I can provide with you all the materials, either from the state attorney's office or from the Court file that I can get again possession of. If that is the problem. Am I understanding you properly?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Galovic, the problem is we do in fact have the material and we tried to find corresponding materials supporting your statistics. But what we have obtained so far from Croatia do not support your statistics. Do you have --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, this has caused more or less, as a matter of fact, Mr. Galovic, you -- apart from answering the question, you also asked yourself what the issue was and why what you had done until now was not sufficient, and then Ms. Mahindaratne responded to that, which is a bit out of the scope of the examination of a witness. So it's understandable that Ms. Mahindaratne responded to what you said. But she'll now put her next question to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, first and foremost, can you tell me what type of material can you provide to support your statistics that you provided yesterday? Are you able to provide crime files?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, yes. It's an enormous undertaking because some of those data are in Knin, some in Gospic and Gradacac, some in Benkovac, some in Zadar, some even in Karlovac, but it is possible. If the entries are not sufficient, then I don't see that should be any problem for us to collect all this information that you are requesting and provide you with it. There's no problem there. I simply couldn't make up these figures and data. The data are as they are. Whatever you wish, you can obtain, but I must caution you - and I've already said that several times - that they are dispersed, the data has been dispersed after the change of jurisdiction to several state attorney's offices. That is why some things do not coincide. But each of them individually are precise and correct, because there's the number of reports of the police. There's a date, there's the name of the person, there is the act, there is the actual crime, and whichever data you request, I can provided you with within a reasonable period of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Are you able to provide us with the work product or the tables that may have been produced in compiling the statistics? For example, in extracting the data from the registers, your clerks may have surely made a record. Are you able to provide us with that record?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may get some clarity. Are we talking about the 1995 statistics or 2006?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: 1995 statistics.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's quite a long time ago, but you will be surprised by my answer. Not much but some, yes. The data written by hand which were later included in this report, I do have them. I have such data.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For these monthly reports sent to the ministry and tables that accompanied them.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So you do have tables, such as the table that we saw a little while ago, supporting your statistics which you could provide to the Trial Chamber. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a sense, yes. They're not identical tables. The tables differ, depending on what you wish to show by a table. The table I'm referring to for this period you can see the quantity of files received and what happened later with those files, the process that was undertaken, the indictments issued and so on. But I'm sorry, I don't understand. If you have this report, is this checking the data? Fine. I do have a part of that, and I can send them to you. In fact, the part referring to these data could be sent to you in a short period of time. You will receive pages written by hand and how those data were extracted and transformed into this report. This is the logical sequence of events.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And do those documents refer to the -- the crime files, the corresponding crime files, so that we be able to undertake an evaluation vis-a-vis your entries in the manner that you have done with your table that was just produced.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me see. If you wish to do a complete check, then it would be best for you to ask me whether I can provide the original files and they contain everything. Then I'll obtain the entire file, either from the court, or my own, if I have it, and I will forward them to you. Because those files were formed after the state attorney's office in the court, if there were -- there was an indictment. And those documents must be part of the file and there can be no dispute about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Galovic. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, the Chamber wonders this is the right time and the right place to explore further investigative facilities that may exist where the Chamber expects you to cross-examine the witness further. Could you please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Galovic, in your chart that we just saw, you note the source of your report, the body that has reported the incident to your office. And that would be -- that's indicated in column 2, the column 1 refers to numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if I could have P -- I give the 65 ter number. 7320. That was exhibit number P2568.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, counsel. And if you could go to the next page, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: In column 1 -- I'm sorry, column 2, you record the -- the source of the criminal report. And we note that in most of the entries you record the source as a police station, and you also indicate the KU number. Now, isn't it correct that when a police station initiates an investigation, that matter is recorded in their own crime registers and a KU number is assigned?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is so. That is precisely this number that appears here. Those are the KU numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Likewise, if you, as a state prosecutor, request the police to undertake an investigation, the police would then record that matter in their own crime registers. This is apart from registration in your own books. They would be recorded in the crime registers of the police station which would be given a KU number; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Partially. Because the KU number is the number of the criminal report. There are various numbers, because every processing doesn't end with a criminal report. I can't tell you exactly how the police numbers its documents, but if I asked the police to conduct an inquiry, then, certainly, that is recorded with a reference to my own number on the letter addressed to them, for them to be able to respond to that same request.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So if the police conducts an investigation, that matter would be essentially registered in the police crime registers; isn't that correct? Please, I'm saying in addition to records maintained by your office.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me correct myself. The police never conducts an investigation. Maybe there's an error in the translation. The police either acts independently or upon instructions from us, and they process the case. They conduct inquiries, and when they establish that there is ground to suspect that a criminal act has been committed, and if the perpetrator is known, then a criminal report is filed with this -- such a number. If they establish that there was a crime committed and they haven't discovered the perpetrator, then it figures under a different number as a report against an unknown person. All this is registered. They have their own register and the state attorney's office has their own register. We have our own records and they have their own, referring to the same problems, the same issues.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have a procedural matter to be raised. I note the time, so perhaps the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then perhaps we already ask Madam Usher to escort Mr. Galovic out of the courtroom. We'll have a break, Mr. Galovic. We'd like to see you back after the break. Ms. Mahindaratne. Oh, Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Thank you. The issue we'd like to put on the record is with respect to expert reports from the Defence. I note the reference in the transcript at 17977 on 3 June where we were told we were going to receive the bulk of expert reports within two weeks. We've had discussion with counsel about this on an ongoing basis. Last week, we asked for -- to get all the reports by 30 June. As the Chamber knows so far, we have received two expert reports: The experts of Mr. Cross and the expert report of Mr. Corn. We have not received any other expert reports. Given the Defence's announcement that they will close their case in the first or second week of September, that reduces the time left for us to prepare for any other experts. Also the recess is coming so many of our staff will be missing. In all fairness to Mr. Kehoe, we have discussed the matter with him several times. He informed us - and he will correct me if I'm wrong - there are two additional expert reports that we may get but that he is waiting for an English translation. Given the late nature now as the Defence case is essentially has three weeks before the recess and two or three weeks after, we would really need disclosure of these report if experts will be called right after the break just so that we can prepare adequately. For example, Mr. Corn's report we received like literally 30 days before he is supposed to testify, or 31 days, and part of this process of negotiating and asking in June and the agreement to give us in advance was the understanding that sometimes more time than 30 days is necessary for these reports. So if we can just put that on the record and have a date by which we can be certain we will get reports for any experts that will be called in the Defence case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. With regard to the report, I think counsel misspoke. That's not Mr. Corn's, that's General Cross' report. I think that that's just clarifying that last bit. General Cross will testify before the break. Any other expert that we have, such as we provided Professor Corn's expert. He is not going to testify until September. The other issue is General Jones. He likewise will not testify till after the break, but his report will be done imminently; and imminently I have within the next few days, the early part of next week the latest I believe. The one problematic report that I talked to Mr. Hedaraly about which he gracefully had mentioned was a report that I got from an expert that literally is somewhere in the area of 60 to 70 pages in Croatian we'll have with attachments, which we are vigorously trying to translate. To be frank with you, Your Honour, I haven't been able to read it myself, and we are, I will tell you, putting all hands on trying to get this translated so we can put it to some use. And I will tell you, Mr. President, that it will not be used prior to the break. I mean, we will, of course, not put it in until -- till the -- well, after the break. I mean, we can gladly give it to them in Croatian now. Out of respect of colleagues, I know they don't speak Croatian either, so that's we've been vigorously trying to get it translated. But that's where we are with regard to that report and that's fueled from Mr. Pokaz.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Jones report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Jones report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Next week, Tuesday? You said a couple of days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's Friday morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My problem, and I know this is not something that is -- my problem right now is this the 4th of July weekend in the United States and people are out and about, so if I can have till Thursday and I will get it by then. Again, he will not be testifying until after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thursday, and no testimony before the recess. Is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Well, it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just talking the Jones report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: It doesn't look like we have choice, Mr. President, in this matter. I mean, we're told that the bulk of the reports we'll get by mid-June. Now we're mid-July we've received two. I mean, I understand there is some problems but that is what the Chamber told us, and we were instructed to raise the matter and we tried to discuss the matter over and over and we asked for 30 June, and we understand that there are obviously problems associated with it. But, it is getting harder and harder to prepare. I know it's after the recess, but during the recess a lot of our team will not be here either. So we're talking about, if we get it next week, two weeks before the recess, and two weeks after the recess, gives us four weeks - maybe one or two in the middle. It's just -- and then if we get other expert reports that got to get translated, then we will end up with three, four, five expert reports, and we'll have a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was not inviting a re-start of the discussion because it is clear what's bothering the Defence and I'm just ... Mr. Kehoe you said the early part of next week. That's Thursday for you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's a different approach of what a week is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I forgot about the 4th of July weekend which Mr. Cronin, my colleague reminded me of. Mr. President, if I could say -- but, I mean, and I'm trying to get this information to the Prosecution as quickly as possible. I mean, we did receive addendums to two reports less than or for 30 days prior to. For instance, Mr. Konings testified. But that's neither here nor there. I am trying to get this report to them as soon as possible. I will tell the Chamber with regard to General Jones' report, we are talking about somewhere 12 to 14 pages tops. This is not some magnum opus for the OTP to get their mind around, so I think that is -- it's going to be quite terse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, you consider the specific circumstances that exist in the United States these days. Let me then also pay attention to the time difference between the United States. In the United States they can work on it for the whole of the Wednesday, which means that the time limit is set at Thursday morning, 9.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For the Jones report. Now the other one. What's the size of the other report? You haven't read it, but you have weighed it, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I have weighed it, Mr. President, and it is -- frankly, it was -- in Croatian it was 60 to 70 pages. I mean, it was double-spaced, but it's still pretty lengthy. I was -- we are feverishly getting any number of people attempting to translate it. And I will tell in all candid --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When did you receive it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think the early part of last week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Early part and late part of weeks is --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I do believe I was told about last [overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Friday or?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, I think I was told about a week of last Monday or Tuesday, one of those days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What portion has been translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'd have to check, Mr. President. I can find that out at the break of how much has been translated. If we can -- just my colleague can send an e-mail back to the Zagreb office and the people in Zagreb who are translating it and see how much we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the structure of the report such that you can identify, well, let's say general conclusions or I have got no idea what the report is, but sometimes you can start translating conclusions and then go to the details later, or leave out the footnotes for the time being so that you prepare, first of all, the body of the -- I'm trying to find a way in which --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I do believe there are conclusions and we can refocus and get conclusions on the various areas. There is a structure. Again, this is what has been told me. There are individual conclusions in that structure, and we can provide those. I just have to -- if can just send an e-mail during the break, and hopefully by the next break we can have more concrete information on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, it's not a way out for the problem. It's just a practical approach that if, for example, you tell us that it would take you another ten or 14 days to have it translated, that we would suggest to you, that already to, in the sequence translation, that you might even gain some advantage by giving priority to certain parts of the report. It's certainly not to offer you a way out that more time could be used for the translation. The Chamber would like to be informed about when you would expect to be able to provide a translation, and also what has been translated over the last ten days, because you apparently are in possession of this report now for ten days. You were in an ongoing discussion with Mr. Hedaraly on timely production of a -- of an expert report. Therefore, the Chamber would like to know what has been done over the last ten days to -- and then we'll further deal with the matter. Any other issue, Mr. Hedaraly?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If I could just confirm that these are the only additional reports we'll be getting; those two?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just those two. I do have one matter that Mr. Hedaraly raised yesterday, and I'm glad that Mr. Hedaraly MFI'd those two documents, because I honestly don't recall what they were, but we have reviewed those documents and have no objection. Whatever those two documents were exactly --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: That's P2566 and P2567.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And can you remind us what these documents are, because they were bar tabled.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: They were bar tabled Mr. Waespi at the end, but the testimony of witness Bilic, which were documents about the -- parts of the documents of the whereabouts of the 15th Home Guard Regiment, which the witness was part of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's correct. And an order and the whereabouts; that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Registrar, the -- P2566 and P2567 are admitted into evidence. We will have a break and resume at five minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Registrar, may I have document number 4460, please. That's a 65 ter a number.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Galovic, isn't it correct that you met with delegates of the Amnesty International during 1997, 1998?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did meet with them a great many times. I don't remember exactly when, but I did meet with representatives of various international organisations.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And the principal purpose of those meetings were to discuss prosecutions conducted by your offices in relation to crimes committed in relation to Operation Storm; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not just that, but that was included.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And you discussed the statistics and prosecutions conducted by you with -- with those delegates; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if you could move to the English translation, page -- this is the English -- it's the original. Page 23, and the Croatian translation page 24. And in the English I'm referring to the first paragraph, which is continuation from the previous page.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Galovic, do you see that paragraph where it's recorded: "The prosecutors in many relevant courts were reluctant or refused to meet with Amnesty International delegates visiting Croatia in May 1998 without express permission of the Ministry of Justice. However, the organisation was able to meet with the prosecutors handling most of the cases of killings committed in former Sector South, the Zadar and Sibenik county courts?" And then it's footnoted, footnote number 12 reads: "In late March 1998, changes to the borders of the Zadar and Sibenik counties went into effect which transferred many municipalities which had been in Zadar county to Sibenik county, including Knin and many others in former Sector South. As a result, ongoing criminal cases also were transferred from the responsibility of the Zadar county prosecutor and court to the Sibenik county prosecutor and court. As a result, the dust has been blown off several outstanding cases, which are now coming to trial in the Sibenik court [sic]."

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And if we could move to the next page, page 24. And in the Croatian version, page 24.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm advised that the witness can't see the footnote or hadn't -- hadn't scrolled down on the B/C/S to see the footnote.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Do you see that footnote, Mr. Galovic? It's right at the top?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were you able to follow what was -- what Ms. Mahindaratne was reading? Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And if we move to the Croatian version, focus on the paragraph right at the bottom, page 24. And in the English version, paragraph 2, in page 24.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: It reads: "Despite the Croatian authorities assurances that instructions had been given to ... relevant courts to pursue prosecutions from Operation Storm as a matter of priority ... Amnesty International can find no indications that in fact this was the case. Some cases where indictments had been issued in 1995 or early 1996 were transferred to the Sibenik county court without a trial date ever having been set. The case of two former soldiers accused of rape noted above being one such example (the indictment was issued in December 1995). Another example is a trial for the killing of Andja and Draginja ... which began in Sibenik in May 1998, although the indictment had been filed by the Zadar county prosecutor in September 1996 - that would have been one of the two cases for which the authorities supplied information that an individual was under investigation in June 1996." Mr. Galovic, this is a report about activities of your office. Now, isn't this report accurate, your -- the indictments you filed in fact were not taken out for trial until the cases were transferred to the Sibenik prosecutor's office; isn't that correct? Did you hear me, sir?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I understand. You want me to tell you what is stated in the report of Amnesty International, for me to interpret it my own way. Is that what you're asking me to do?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, my question was, isn't it correct that the indictments that you proffered were not in fact as it's reported here, taken out for trial in the -- until they were transferred to the Sibenik prosecutor's office. This is an accurate report, isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you have misunderstood it. Because a trial is not decided by me. I complete my duty once I issued the indictment. So it says even though the attorney sent the indictment to the court at such and such a date, it's up to the court to continue the proceedings. As a state attorney, I have no influence over the decisions of the court.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Let me also take you to another portion of this report, Mr. Galovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And if we could move to page 19 of the English, the original, and the Croatian version, page 19, Mr. Registrar. And in the Croatian version, it's focussing on the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, just for the record, when you're referring to pages you are referring to e-court pages and not the paging as we find it on the top of the -- each page of the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, can I please have the 65 ter number one more time. It was not -- it was mistranscribed in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And if we could just scroll down to the bottom of the page and the -- do you note that paragraph, Mr. Galovic, which says: "The response is typical in so far as it is vaguely refers to an enormous number of criminal prosecutions with no indication of how, if at all, the specific concern fits into those numbers. Depending on when the letters were issued and by whom, the statistics varied. In correspondence with Amnesty International and in other international fora [phoen] the authorities clearly intended to convey that these investigations and criminal proceedings was sufficient to address the human rights violations and other acts of violence committed in the wake of Operation Storm." And if you could move to page 21, Mr. Registrar, on the English version on e-court, and Croatian version it's page 21, paragraph 2. It says: "Of these 2.849 cases, which the authorities claim were before the courts in June 1996, less than two per cent concerned cases of killings for the criminal act of murder." Then Article 34 of the Croatian Criminal Code: "The authorities claimed that 22 individuals were under investigation, the legal proceedings were under way against 30 people, and that final decisions had been made against one person. When Amnesty International spoke to prosecutors in May 1998 and inquired about why, when in some of the cases the perpetrators had been on active duty with the military or police, they had not been charged with crimes against a civilian population" -- then the act is referred to "Article 120 of the Croatian Criminal Code and the criminal act under Croatian law with which soldiers who had been serving with the RSK army are normally charged if the act involves the killing of civilian. The prosecutors were unable to provide a response. Amnesty International fears that the reason may be political given the widely cited comment of Milan Vukovic, president of the supreme court of Croatia, to the effect that Croatians by definition cannot commit war crimes since they were defending the homeland." And on the same page, if you go to the last paragraph on the English version, in the Croatian version also bottom of the page. I'm sorry, Croatian version page 22 on e-court. I'm reading from the second line from the bottom.
