"And in fact during that meeting, while the justice minister did provide Amnesty International with a breakdown of the statistics which reflected the numbers of individuals charged with particular offences before particular courts, the [indiscernible] of the Justice Ministry noted that these statistics do not in fact solely relate to criminal acts committed in 1995, but represents the criminal cases which are currently before the courts in the relevant regions. The Ministry of Justice representatives confirms that there is no way to discern from the statistics provided which cases were for acts committed in 1995 and which are for acts committed in, for example, 1996 or 1997, nor is it possible to conclude any information about who the victims or suspects might be." Now, this is what we have been discussing, Mr. Galovic. Isn't it correct that today you're unable to just the same way, when you met the delegates of Amnesty International way back, you are unable to in fact accurately provide information to the Trial Chamber to establish that the statistics you provided are for crimes committed in 1995, specifically for August and September 1995; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not correct. Simply, it is not correct. What you have read out doesn't relate it me. It is the impression of Amnesty International linked to proceedings in the whole country. Many comments referred to the work of the ministry. I personally, for each and every criminal act, I'm ready to provide all data and to provide answers, regardless of the question, be they factual or legal questions, for any criminal act, and specifically for killings. And specifically linked to why an act was qualified as being this or that. So for each individual case I'm ready to provide answers.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Galovic, my question is not whether you are ready but you are unable today in the course --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, I object to the commentary by counsel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, I said that I am able to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Galovic, my question is you're unable today, or in the course of your testimony before this Trial Chamber, to provide this Trial Chamber with the required information to support that the statistics you have provided in fact relate to crimes committed in August and September 1995; isn't that correct? In the course of these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you would want me to take out this pile of papers supporting the documentation, you are right. What I am not able to do, really, is from where I'm sitting now to present to you the supporting material, the mound of material. You are quite right in that. However, I am happy to provide with you any answers to any of the cases or any reports, be they from Amnesty International or anybody else who talked to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I move this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, in theory I have no objection. If I could just take a look at an appropriate time. If we could get an MFI it real quick.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Can I register my concerns at this point on behalf of the Defence team for Mr. Cermak. The reality of this document is that it's a 60-page Amnesty International report. It's not being tendered through an Amnesty witness or through someone who could speak to how it has been prepared. It is analogous to some of the reports that were dealt with through, for example, Mr. Puhovski who could actually speak to the report. It cover a plethora of issues, including crimes that were allegedly committed in the region. And we have had no opportunity, of course, to cross-examine the maker or preparer of this report. So in our submission it falls into the category of case of an NGO report, and it's not appropriate in the circumstances that we face today with this witness who can speak to merely portions, most of which, if not all, he doesn't accept. In my submission the more appropriate way of dealing with this would be to consider the admission of those portions that Ms. Mahindaratne has dealt with with the witness, to that I would have no objection. But to the entirety of the report which actually also deals with key allegations in this case, including the allegation of Grubori, and I would object to the admission of the entire report, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I not only join in that objection, but for all the discussion of the lack of underlying documentation, we have no documentation for this what report. What underlying documents Amnesty International reviewed, what underlying information they had to base their report on, so I think it's quite hypocritical to criticise this particular witness on the issue of not having his documentation for which his tables were the result of, and when we have bold accusations in this Amnesty International report, without any way to verify, cross-examine, review the underlying documentation ourselves for this particular report. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I don't know whether the witness was criticised or whether questions were put to him as to the availability immediately at this moment on the supporting data. But apart from that, the first issue, Ms. Mahindaratne, apart from other concerns expressed by the Cermak and Markac Defence, are you willing to limit the -- are you willing to limit the evidence to those portions of this document you dealt with, with the witness, leaving the others -- parts out?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President for the reason there are other -- I don't know want to take the time of Court, but there are other portions that's relevant to this witness included in this report. Further, the Defence has in fact tendered, you know, for example Mr. Sekulic's book without calling him to testify and gone through several other, for example, the book by Mr. Marko Vrcelj, then there are other -- this practice has been followed by the Defence in -- during the Prosecution phase of the case, Mr. President. My intention in tendering this is apart from the excerpts that I just read out, there are other information which is relevant to this witness's testimony with regard to the statistics and data.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but then, of course, we would at least need to know which portions you are referring to, because I do understand that again the Chamber has not seen the whole of the report, that if, for example the Grubori incident is dealt with, which may or may not have to do anything with statistics, that Mr. Kuzmanovic objects against at least those portions. So you can approach it from a negative way or from a positive way that you have to identify positively the portions you'd like to seek --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I could do that Mr. President -- not immediately, but I could identify and then perhaps we could just tender those excerpts in -- of the entire report if that is preferable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well if you -- if you have not done that yet, and to the extent the Defence would want to put questions to the witness in relation to those portions, then, of course, it could not be done after the witness has left The Hague. So if you would like to do something of the kind, it should be done at its latest during the next break.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'll do that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we have it, then, for the time being marked for identification, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Awaiting a further selection of portions of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I just on that score, Ms. Mahindaratne's comment on page 50, line 6, if there in fact other portions of this report that are relevant to Mr. Galovic under 90(H), the Prosecution has the obligation to put that to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it -- if other portions are relevant it should be verified with the witness whether -- I don't know what the reports comment on what he said, whether he said certain things or not. But you should, to start with, identify the relevant portions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I will do that Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And whether it should be put to the witness depends on whether the testimony of the witness in any way contradicts the Prosecution's case because that's the test under Rule 90(H).

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not knowing what portions of the document are relevant, of course, it's impossible to say at this moment whether that is the case or not. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if it could be assigned a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit P2569, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I will come -- come to that particular subject later on, Mr. Galovic. Just moving on to the case of Varivode and Gosici, which you discussed yesterday with Mr. Kehoe. And you are aware that the charges in that case has been dropped; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in my case. Charges were dropped once the case was transferred to Sibenik and after my appeal was upheld before the supreme court and admitted that facts were erroneously established, remanded the case to the court, which in this case was the court in Sibenik, where, unfortunately, my colleague, my counterpart withdrew the charges.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That's what I meant. I should have, you know, elaborated by whom. Now, in your statement at pages 6 to 10, you in fact address this particular crime. Now, isn't it correct that this judgement, the judgement provided --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And if I could have in the meanwhile, Mr. Registrar, P1076, please, the judgement itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Galovic, the judgement will be on the screen in a moment and you will be very familiar with that since you appealed against it. Now, this judgement relates to a consolidated trial relating to four separate killing incidents; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: All together eight persons were indicted in that consolidated trial; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes. It was consolidated by the court. It is only the court that can decide about consolidating, joining cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, in the indictments you proffered and, we have those indictments if you want to look at them, but you're probably more familiar about -- you're familiar with them. You have described the -- all the eight accused as civilians. In fact, you have -- addressing that issue in your statement at page 9 you have stated as follows. You have been questioned about that and you say: "Reading the indictment for Gosici I realised that Ivica Petric," I'm sorry, I think that was corrected. Pero Perkovic, yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, the sentence was corrected. Reading the indictment of Gosici, I realised that the Visa Petric and Slatko Ladovic were not members of the HV at the time the criminal offence was perpetrated. And the next sentence should be "Pero Perkovic" not "Ivica Petric."

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: "Pero Perkovic and Nikola Rasic were members of the HV; however, they had days off. But I'm certain that Ivica Petric and Nikola Rasic were only formally HV members and that this status was formally terminated at that point when the indictment was raised," which is why, according to Article 1 of the decree on amendment and supplement of the decree on the organisation, and you refer to the -- the law. You say: "When the military status of the perpetrator of criminal offences criminal" -- this is not correctly recorded. I'm just reading verbatim. "Criminal proceedings terminated before the charges were raised, the trial shall be conducted before the municipal district court having jurisdiction, and in this case the county court in Zadar had jurisdiction for the trial." Now, isn't it correct, Mr. Galovic, that seven out of eight of these persons, and I would tell you exactly whom with the exception of the sixth accused, all the other accused were in fact members of the HV at the time the alleged offences relevant to this indictment were committed?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that a question?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot agree with you. And I can explain why. Operation Storm ceased in my area on the 7th. The situation in the army was all but clear. For the purposes of Storm people from the reserve force were mobilised, and following Operation Storm, it was down to the military administration and the pace of their work on which their mobilisation of these people depended. The military courts were provisional courts, and that is why soon thereafter they were abolished, did not have the necessary human and technical resources to keep up with the situation. If the status of any individual was at any point in time questionable, actions have to be taken speedily. Under our legislation, such swift investigations that have to be carried out can even be carried out by the court that does not have jurisdiction simply to expedite proceedings because that's the central matter. However, the important matter is the following. In every situation, if the individuals concerned have been demobilised before the indictment is issued, they fall under the jurisdiction of a civilian court. Therefore, in any case, they would have been tried before a civilian court. Now, the issue of subject-matter jurisdiction is something that lies solely within the powers of the court. I have no say in that. Before the supreme court or before the county court, the subject-matter jurisdiction was never called into question. If I may only add this, two out of the eight persons were accused of 16 crimes of aggravated murder, murder each, in all 32 crimes of aggravated murder. As for the rest, depending on the crimes they participated, in they were charged with seven and nine crimes of aggravated murder respectively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. If we could check the word the witness used at page 54 line 19, that first word I believe would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, could I.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Galovic, let me just find it. Yes. You said it was down to the military administration, and the pace of their work on which their ... and then what did you say in relation it persons? You said --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that these persons were certainly not members of the Croatian armed forces any longer. They were no longer soldiers. That is my position. And this proved true later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not re-stating the content the. The transcript reads at this moment: "It was down to the military administration and the pace of their work on which their" -- as it reads now, "mobilisation of these people depended," where logically one would expect "demobilisation." What did you say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Demobilisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The matter has been clarified. Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Galovic, that wasn't my question. My question was at the time the alleged crimes were committed, the accused, with the exception of the sixth accused, all the others were members of the HV. My question was at the time the offence were committed, the accused were members of the HV; isn't that correct? You are aware of that, isn't it.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not, but I cannot say that they were not. I don't know. I took such activities as I was bound to take under the law, which included the request for the conduct of an investigation and the request for detention, which the court granted. We did not have time to try and ascertain whether they were members of the army or not. My position is, still today, that to all intents and purposes they never were members of the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Galovic. Let me in fact point out that material. You are aware that all eight accused testified before the court in this trial; isn't it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that, but I have no reason to doubt that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, I think the witness is confusing the actual trial in the Zadar court as opposed to here because the question is it was testified that: "You were aware that all eight accused testified before the court in this trial?"

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, let me be specific.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Galovic, you're aware that the accused testified before the Zadar county court in the trial which you conducted against them. You are aware of that, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what confused me. They do not testify. They were accused. They presented their Defence. That's what confused me. Under our law, they present their Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Perhaps I'm using the wrong terminology vis-a-vis how you understand. Do you know that in fact one of those accused testified before this Trial Chamber; in fact, two days back.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, let me first take you to, on this judgement.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if you could move to -- in English version page 9, and the Croatian version, page 11. And if you could just focus on paragraph 2 of the Croatian version.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: This is a statement by the first accused, Nikola Rasic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I think we're on the wrong page of the English version. Page 9.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And this is what Nikola Rasic said before the Zadar court about his -- what he was doing at the time of the crime, Mr. Galovic. He says: "He took part in Operation Storm volunteering in Skradin after he heard that it was being prepared. There he was issued with an automatic rifle and equipment. In that operation, he took part in attacks on Ljubicici and Tepsici, where his commander was accused Mijic. During the Operation Storm, he advanced in the direction of Kistanje."

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And if we could move to -- in the Croatian version it goes on to the next page. And in the English version if we could move to the next page, Mr. Registrar. And if you could go up on the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: It says: "Upon the presentation of the incriminating evidence relating to the murder committed on 20th August, 1995, in Ocestovo near Knin," that's one of the crimes related to this consolidated indictment, "when the victim Savo Solaja was killed, he stated that it was true that he had been in Ocestovo that day because he was issued a command by Gojevic that morning to more towards Srb." Now this reflects that not only was the first accused a member of the HV at the time of the offence, but he was in fact on duty, wasn't he, quite contrary to what have you stated in --

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true, if you believe what he says. He was an accused, and, under our law, he was entitled to defend himself whatever way he wanted, including by lying. On the other hand, what else can you expect from an individual who had been charged with 16 murders, but that he would say that -- of course, he wouldn't say that he did that from -- for the -- venting his base instincts to kill old women, et cetera. Of course, he said that it was his duty as a member of the Croatian Army. That was his Defence which I would never accept without verifying it first in detail. In this particular case it was not relevant, because nobody deployed him over there, if anybody did, to kill and loot. Such Defences that they devised subsequently I never trusted nor did my deputy who worked with me. Somebody who killed nine individuals cannot be treated as a credible individual. That's my view. In every word they utter, they will boast by saying that they were performing their military duty. That is another way of enabling themselves to look at themselves in the mirror by saying that you were a patriot doing your duty rather than merely a robber killing people.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Galovic, what is the information that you were provided with which in fact indicated to you that these persons were not members of the HV at the time of the crime?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't want to go back to the time of the commission of the crime because I said that, at that point, all steps needed to be taken to preserve evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Galovic --

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Could you please answer my question. My question was: What is the information that was provided to you that, in fact, contradicted this, that indicated to you that they were not in fact members of the HV at the time the crime was committed? What is the information that was given to you that made -- renders this -- [indiscernible].

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From their overall conduct and their statements, from having observed the entire group, it became clear that to say the at least their status was questionable. That was not, however, the time to deal with their status. We were supposed to address the crimes they committed. That's what I saw as my duty.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Did you --

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had it subsequently turned out that they were members of the HV, then it would be down -- up to the court to decide who had jurisdiction over them. It was not down to me to decide on the jurisdiction. It was up to the court, if you will. It was up to the court structure all the way to the supreme court to deal with their status. I was interested in establishing if they committed the offence or not. That was what I was dealing with at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Galovic, did you in fact in preparing to submit the indictment or conduct investigations call for information from the military police or from the military to establish what their status was on the date of the crime?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The day that we learnt about it, it meant that a criminal report should be filed and that simultaneously those persons are taken up by the investigating judge, that the proceedings had to be initiated, because, if we within the deadline of 24 hours you don't start proceedings they are released. Afterwards, all the questions you're putting to me were within that competence of the court and not mine. And, after all, no one had any remarks or objections regarding this, afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Let me just quickly read out some other excerpts, Mr. Galovic, and then I will ask you a question. I don't want to go through the reading the entire -- of all of the other accused, but for the record, Mr. President, the second accused --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's try to --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'll just give the page numbers, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You want to put to the witness that the other accused also told the court that they were on active duty when these crimes were committed. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's keep matters rather simple. Are you aware, Mr. Galovic, that the other accused have given similar statements when defending themselves at trial?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apparently the factual basis for, I take it, the question --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- is there. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if you could just go to page 16 of the English version and in the Croatian version page 27. I'm sorry, if you could go to page 18 of the English version. And page 29 of the Croatian version.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Galovic, now, you studied this judgement in considering appealing against it; isn't that correct? This is what the seventh accused stated in front of the Zadar county court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, I think the witness was asked to -- I think he was nodding yes and there is no response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It has now been confirmed that his body language was affirmative. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now this is what he has stated. He says: "Although the fact that he was in the area of Bosnia at the front from 3 to 11 October 1995 is not contentious, it is not clear to him why these criminal proceedings make it necessary to falsify the date of his demobilisation as being on 25th September and not as it should be on 17 October 1995. He connects this with threats from the police, but he will no longer be a Croatian soldier and this behaviour insulted him specifically. He took part in Operation Storm from the very beginning."

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if you could move to page 20 -- sorry, page 21 of the English version. And the Croatian version, page 31, focussing on paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: This is what the eighth accused said before court. "After the terrain near Drvar, he was given five or six days of leave. And on 1st October, 1995, he was to have headed towards Mrkonjic Grad where they set off on 3rd October and were there until 13th October. It is easily possible to check in the unit that he had returned from the front on 13th October, and it is therefore improper that the police forces falsified his demobilisation date in order to make it appear that in the period the police is interested in, he was not a soldier." Now, Mr. Galovic, when you saw those references, were you not concerned that a formal military process may have in fact been abused to cover up a crime or to make these accused appear as being civilians on the date of the crime? Were you not concerned when you read those portions in the judgement?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On condition that I did read them, certainly it is disturbing. But let me say, once again, that this fully confirms all that I have said in relation to what I considered to be relevant, whether, at the time of the indictment, they were civilians or not. I'm not talking about the date of the perpetration of the act. I said that even if they were soldiers, in the procedural sense, this doesn't change anything. It was our duty to take the steps we took and after that, to continue the proceedings as we had started them before a civilian court because in the meantime they had been demobilised. So it's quite irrelevant for the procedure whether this was in October or in September. Now, as I personally was not in charge of the case, I cannot tell you, but I can check if there is anything that can be checked with regard to the records, because, after all, this is also part of Defence of the accused.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, when I asked you whether Mr. Pero Perkovic had testified here you said you knew about it. How did you know about it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I watched it on the Internet, or part of it, most of his testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you. And in fact I would like to show you a document.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That would be 2556, Mr. Registrar, if could you call that up on the -- I'm sorry, it's Exhibit P2556.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And this is in fact --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, you read from page 21 in English. On page 20 of the judgement, I read: "The eighth accused, Nedeljko Mijic, defends him with ..." and what then follows is apparently what he submit to the court. You are talking about whether you are disturbed by reading this in a judgement, but is it a proper understanding of this part of the judgement that it reflects what the Defence of the accused was?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not any finding of the court.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. My point was whether in fact the witness took note of it and acted upon it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the witness has earlier given his views on the interest an accused may have in putting forward such a Defence. You may proceed. I just wanted to be clear that there's no misunderstanding of what was read to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, because I pointed out that these are confessions made by -- not confessions, the testimony of the accused before the Zadar county court. In fact, Your Honour, in fact, with the -- the position to the witness that all the other --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, if --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If we could have, Mr. Registrar, Exhibit P2556.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, in a moment, Mr. Galovic, you will see on the screen the record of interrogation of the accused Pero Perkovic. In fact, this is one of the documents that you considered for -- in contemplating the indictment; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Do you notice that in the section where the personal details of Mr. Perkovic is noted, about the ninth line it says: "He's a member of HV Croatian Army from July 1991 to 25th September 1995 with only two-month break, 113th Brigade." I don't know whether on the Croatian -- can you see it in the Croatian document?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So in fact the documentation that you considered in contemplating the indictment itself records the accused as being members of the HV; whereas, in this court, you indicated that you were not certain about the status.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I answer now?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but it says here clearly that he was a member until the 25th of September, 1995, and the indictment was issued in February 1996. I have already said on several occasions that a person who is demobilised, even if he was -- even if he had been a soldier when the crime was committed, it is the civilian court who -- that has jurisdiction over this person, and this confirms precisely what I have been saying. It says the 25th of September, 1995, and I accept this as an accurate date.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Let me in fact call up a document right now.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If I can have P1007, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Galovic, your position is that if a soldier who has committed a crime is demobilised before the charges, he is considered as a civilian. In fact, let me show you the code of military discipline of the HV. In fact, the military itself does not endorse what you are saying. And if we could move to Article --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, your line "... he is considered as a civilian," is a complex one. What I heard the witness tell us is that prosecution and trial takes place before a civilian court, whether he is then considered as a civilian is a different matter, but for that purpose, that's what I heard the witness say. I also heard the witness say that sometimes it was difficult to establish whether, due to demobilisation, people were still or were not anymore members of the HV, but I did not hear him say that if demobilised before the charges were brought, that he was considered to be a civilian, and especially since you do not refer us to -- refer to this status in any time-frame. I have some difficulties in fully understanding this observation which apparently precedes your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, let me just put two questions before that thing and to make it clear and make the point as clear, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, in the indictment, Mr. Galovic, I'm not taking issue with the fact that the accused were in fact tried in a civilian court. But in the indictments, you do not, in fact, mention the fact that the accused were in fact members of the HV at the time the crime was committed. Their, in fact, civilian status is described. In fact if we -- if you want to go back to the indictments, there is not a singular reference that they were members of the military at the time the crime was committed; isn't that correct? If could you say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not fully. If when looking at the judgement, which I did recently, there's no mention of their status, except in one case, in the case of Hrstic and Petric.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Galovic, I'm not talking about the judgement. In your indictments have you not mentioned any --

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The indictment, in the factual description -- the factual description of the judgement is identical to the factual description in the indictment, but if you wish I will speak about the indictment. In relation to the murder of Canak, I think, my deputy said that they were engaged in some kind of an action, and that is when they killed Petric and Hrstic, so you can check that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Galovic, please, my point is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, the witness is answering her question. She may not like it, but she [sic] is answering the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne specifically asks -- Ms. Mahindaratne specifically asks whether membership of the HV was mentioned in the indictment against the accused in this case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In one case, it was. What I have just been saying, in relation to the killing of Djuradj Canak, for Petric and Hrstic. In other cases, no mention was made of their status, whether they were civilians or military personnel, but just the fact that they committed a crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If you could now, I'm not in fact -- the issue is not about where they were tried, Mr. Galovic. But the issue is that the indictments do not divulge the fact that they were members of the HV at the time the crime was committed and as such, isn't it correct, if one were to provide statistics of the crimes committed by military personnel, as opposed to civilians, your documentation would in fact be misleading?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, first of all, I object to the form of this question, because again counsel is giving a speech for the first four lines. If we can just limit this to a question as opposed to the prefatory comments, I think that would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, wouldn't it be true that -- I think the witness explained to us that it's -- whether someone was demobilised or not was a rather confusing matter in that point of time. The witness also explained to us that accused had a certain interest in presenting themselves as active military personnel. Now, if you want to say that if wrongly someone was qualified as a civilian or a military, that this might have had consequences for the statistics, to the extent the statistics would pay attention to the status of an accused, whether it's misleading or not depends on whether it's wrong or not. It misleads if it's wrong; it doesn't mislead if it's right. I think we have spent quite some time on what the status of the persons was. I think we have spent some time on -- on the basis of the knowledge of this witness, what decisions were taken at the time to bring them before the court. These last questions do not really assist the Chamber in making the determinations.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President, I will move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If we could move to page 2, the English version, and Croatian version, page -- yeah, page 2 in the Croatian version also. And focus on Article 2. I'm sorry, if could you move to the next page, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you could see --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If you could focus on Article 4, I think, on the Croatian version, it's page two; that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: The Article reads as follows, Mr. Galovic, you can see: "The following persons serving notice armed forces may be held liable for violations of the Code of Military Discipline."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne. Yes, now we have the -- yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: "... violations of Code of Military Discipline: 1, servicemen; 2, civilians serving in the armed forces (herein after civilians serving in the armed forces). "Even after termination of services in the armed forces persons under the paragraph 1 of this Article shall continue to be responsible for the violation of the Code of Military Discipline committed during their service as determined by this Code." So isn't it correct -- my question to you, Mr. Galovic, is in order for the military to be able to discipline a member of the HV, even those who have been demobilised, but if the crime had been committed when they were members of the HV, they would have to have information that a person has been convicted in a criminal process.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, we're dealing with military discipline.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, it is perfectly clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So my question to you is: Was there a process in which the civilian courts, upon convicting members of the military who had committed crimes but who had been demobilised before indictment, and after a process in the civilian courts having convicted, was there a process for the civilian courts of your office to inform the military in order to -- so that they could take disciplinary measures under this Article, Article 4. How would the military know that in fact a member of the HV who had committed a crime has been tried for a serious crime in a civilian court, if in fact he had been demobilised before indictment but after the crime?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say, as a matter of principle, that the criminal proceedings should include disciplinary proceedings. This doesn't exclude a disciplinary proceedings but it's something quite different, and it has nothing in common with criminal proceedings and court proceedings, and the court has no obligation to initiate any such thing. This is initiated by the disciplinary judge within the army if interested. He looks for information, because this is mostly known. If he intends to start the disciplinary proceedings, then the disciplinary judge from the disciplinary court will look for the data that he needs if he needs such information. However, in criminal proceedings that is never done, because a criminal proceeding should consume everything that was part of a disciplinary procedure.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Let me just move on. Now, are you a aware, Mr. Galovic, that in the Varivode/Gosici trial all the accused claimed that they had in fact been threatened and their confessions were obtained under duress?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I know. But they claimed that this was done to them by police. However, what we based our indictment on were their Defences before the investigating judge, because what is stated in the police, according to our law to this day, is not evidence. Statements made to the police are just the material for starting proceedings. After this statement to the police, they were taken to the investigating judge, and then they said what they said in their Defence. In two cases almost complete confession -- in two cases a complete confession and in one a partial confession, and that is what we were guided by. This whole story about duress and threats started several days later when one of the accused asked to be seen by the investigating judge again for him to tell him his story once again, and all I can say is that he had no other thing to resort to, because how else will you defend yourself, unless you say that you were threatened and forced to make a confession under duress.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now do you know, Mr. Galovic, that Mr. Perkovic in fact testified that he made the statement to the investigating judge, that this very -- the same day that he was interrogated by the police. Do you know that? He testified to that effect in -- before this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the problem is, even if he didn't make the statement on the same day. They all made statements very shortly after the statements to the police because the deadlines are short. They first made the statement to the investigating judge, and after that, he made a decision to conduct an investigation and to hold them on -- in remand. That is the procedure. There could be no other.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, isn't that correct, Mr. Galovic, that the Trial Chamber in Zadar - I'm just referring to the Zadar county court - acquitted the accused on the basis that those confessions were considered unreliable because they did not correspond to the material evidence in the case, the -- the accounts given by the eye-witnesses and the other physical observations on the ground. Isn't that correct? That was one of the basis on which the court rejected those confessions? Did you hear me?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct, the court in the first instance acquitted them. However, on appeal the supreme court -- on our appeal the supreme court overturned the first instance decision and remanded the case for a re-trial. And the supreme court referred, in fact, to the confessions by the accused as mentioned in the first instance judgement. That was the basis for which the supreme court in fact upheld the convictions, in respect of Petric and Rasic in that case. And, unfortunately --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: We'll --

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- on that same basis the supreme court rejected our appeals against sentences.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: We'll -- in fact, I will tender the supreme court judgement later on, Mr. Galovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could have the judgement again, P1076 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, I'm also looking at the clock. Would you give us an estimate on the time you would still need.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I may perhaps need about -- a substantial amount of the next session. Perhaps ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I inquire with the Defence teams.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Frankly, Mr. President, right now I'd be very brief. I'd say, you know, five minutes or so, maybe a few minutes more, but not much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Higgins.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I don't currently anticipate anything, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Likewise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, we'll first have a break. It's approximately time for a break. We want the testimony of this witness to be concluded today.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which practically means that you have half an hour after the break. And if it would be 35 minutes that would not bring us into great problems. The Chamber would very much like to you continue your cross-examination in a focussed and organised way, in which repetitions are avoided. We'll have a break, and we'll resume at ten minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Galovic, isn't it correct that in the Varivode/Gosici trial process, the -- the ballistic analysis on the shell casings found at the scene did not match the weapons seized from the accused?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Isn't it correct that the witnesses to the incident did not identify the accused as having been at the scene of crime?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You are aware that --

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that they were not not at the scene of crime. They were there and admitted to that, but nobody identified them, and that is much is true.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That was my question. And isn't it correct that Mr. Zganjer, the Sibenik county prosecutor, upon getting the case back for re-trial, dropped the charges on the same grounds on which the Trial Chamber, in fact, rejected the confessions, as being unreliable?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was Mr. Zganjer's decision, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the documents in relation to this section shall be bar tabled later on, due to lack of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that will are be no --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I don't know, Mr. President. To the extent there are matters in there that go to the Defence -- the -- the OTP's case, I mean, they're still responsible to put those issues to the witness so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But usually court-related materials.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I agree with Mr. President. I don't know if that's what we're talking about. Are we simply talking about just court-related material?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That's it, Mr. President. There is nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, if -- if -- my next statement of that is if the Prosecution at some point is going to argue things that Mr. Galovic did or did not do that are contained in those documents, then they still have the obligation to put it to Mr. Galovic now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Galovic, did you consider the discrepancies vis-a-vis -- between the material evidence and the confessions of these accused in contemplating your charges? Did you consider the fact that the ballistic analysis did not match the weapons seized from the accused, did you consider the fact that there were no identification of the accused, did you consider the fact that the versions provided by the witnesses did not correspond to the witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, I think that's three questions. I object to the form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, although this witness has shown to be perfectly able to identify the several parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I withdraw the objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Galovic, could you please answer the questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I took all of this into consideration. On the issue of ballistic examination, I have to tell yo, that there was among the bullet casings such material that could indicate whether certain weapons were fired from or not. However, the material was quite damaged, and the examiner said that it was difficult to determine if the weapons were fired from or not. However, still, this did not mean that the perpetrators could not be established. Furthermore, there were so many weapons around that it was not possible with precision to rule out that certain weapons were used, and no specific findings were made in relation to that. There is an number of -- what we referred to as indirect evidence on the basis of which I made rulings, and I stand by them. What was among the findings of the ballistic expertise does not support the decision but does not exclude the decisions that were made in respect of the accused. I wanted to follow up on that; however, this was no longer within my jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Galovic, do you know that the Sibenik prosecutor, Mr. Zganjer - he, in fact, testified here - upon decision to drop the charges, he initiated a investigation to find out who the actual perpetrators were; and in the course of that investigation, he found that the military police company in Sibenik had suppressed the investigation, in order to protect the actual perpetrators. Were you aware that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object. That is not what he said. I mean, does he have a line in -- reference in his testimony where he said exactly that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Transcript reference: T.11542 to T.11544. Mr. President, T.11542 to 544.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you perhaps read to the witness what the testimony was. Let me just see ...

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Let me read it, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: "Having taken over the case, I analysed the evidence and established that there was no reliable evidence to proceed against those accused who had been indicted in the case. I discussed this with the state attorney for Croatia and his deputies. And received his approval to dismiss the case against the five persons who had been indicted. I'm not aware of any other persons being tried for the crimes after that, I believe if the military police officers Simic had been allowed to carry out the investigation including ballistic investigation in October 1995 as planned, the real perpetrators of the crime could have been identified." Then it goes on to ... "Goran Vunic, as far as that case filed is concerned, and I stress the case file, was not mentioned as a person who would be under suspicion" --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, where are you reading from counsel?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: "... was not mentioned an as person who would be under suspicion this way or the other. When is it that the name of Goran Vunic ultimately emerges? When I decided to desist the criminal prosecution of those suspects, the following question arose. If -- as I was deeply convinced those persons were not the perpetrators, who was it that killed the 17 individuals. At that point for a state attorney the proceedings against those accused ended. However" -- and it goes on. "... [indiscernible] led me to learn in 2002 that for certain reasons, the commander of the military police company in Sibenik Nenad Mrkota had obstructed the activity of the military police of Damir Simic. It was at that point that the suspicion arose, which made me believe that Goran Vunic could be the possible perpetrator of the events in Gosici and Varivode."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, were you able to follow the portions of the testimony that were read to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, did you ever have that information, that --

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was no reason why I should learn that. You asked me if I knew that Mr. Zganjer had established. From what you've just read out, I did not observe him establish anything. Had he established something, then it would have been only logical for that person to be prosecuted.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Let me tell you, Mr. Galovic, in fact Mr. Damir Simic, the head of crime section of the Sibenik police testified in these proceedings, and he confirmed and he in fact testified to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, can we have a page and reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, the tone as such, Do you have a page reference. If you can just --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Respectfully --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I respectfully need page reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I will just direct counsel to P971, which is in evidence, with the entire note is about the issue of interference.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, in fact the head of crime section of the military police in Sibenik testified that when he attempted to investigate a suspect, in relation to the Gosici/Varivode killings, his company commander interfered with that investigation and stopped him from proceeding. This in fact -- isn't that correct, Mr. Galovic, that -- that reflects that your -- the basis on which you indicted the suspects were not grounded on a complete investigation into the crime?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. My position remains as it has always been, and there is Mr. Zganjer's position.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now isn't it correct, Mr. Galovic, moving on to another area, that when the police receives information of serious crime, particularly in the case of killing incidents, they have to report the matter to the investigative judge and yourself?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, yes. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That same rule applies to -- applies where a human corpse is covered; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, they would inform me of all such situations. If the corpse belongs to a person who was killed, in that case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I have document P -- Exhibit P1061, please, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, isn't it right, Mr. Galovic, that you never received a report from the police regarding the killings in Grubori hamlet in the Plavno area on 25th August 1995?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. I never received it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You have in fact confirmed that fact by this report to the state attorney.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, isn't it correct that during the time the Grubori incident was -- received publicity on TV and in the press?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What period of time are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: In August 1995 just soon after the killings in Grubori.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know. But when did it receive publicity?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: In August 1995.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Publicity? How? When I didn't know of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: In fact this Trial Chamber has seen video footage of General Cermak being interviewed by a journalist from HTV.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I object to this line of questioning. The witness was asked specifically whether he knew of publicity at the time. The witness gave an answer which clearly indicated that he didn't. It's therefore wrong of Ms. Mahindarante to then try and again suborn the witness by making reference to video footage in this manner, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That objection is denied. It was in the margin of an answer that the witness said something about it, and Ms. Mahindaratne is entitled to further explore the matter, although within certain limits, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, did you see that interview on HTV where General Cermak was interviewed about what happened in Grubori. This Trial Chamber has viewed it. Did you see it? It was two days after the incident that he was interviewed?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Let me ask to show you, Mr. Galovic, a press clipping of the incident which was published in Slobodna Dalmacija, newspaper.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If I could have, Mr. Registrar, P1050 which is not -- which is marked but not admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: At this stage, could I ask that a foundation be laid as to whether this witness at that particular time saw any media articles relating to this incident?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Let me ask you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, one second. Ms. Mahindaratne may approach this evidentiary issue as she wishes, against whether we go from the general to the specific or from the specific to the general is up to her. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If I could have that document on the screen, Mr. Registrar, P1050, marked but not admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, what you are seeing, Mr. Galovic, is a press article about this incident which was published on 29th August in this newspaper. Now, is it your position that you never saw any press reports of this incident during the time?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, I didn't. I would dearly like to know what the article says. I didn't see that. I didn't see such an article.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: When did you first learn of the incident?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it had to do with the publication of information of the Helsinki Committee. When they gathered and published their information, I came to know about the killings in Grubori. I knew about Gosici and Varivode. We discussed that. But I didn't know about Grubori, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And when was that? When -- when did you read this --

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When did I learn about it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was no longer within my competence. It was within the competence of Sibenik.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Galovic, you are not --

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw that the first document you showed me was from 2003.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You did not answer my question. I said when -- give us a time-frame when you learned of the incident in Grubori. If you could give us a year and a month, or even just a year.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not how you put the question, and cannot give you the exact year. I don't know. I tie it up with the report of the Helsinki Committee. I said that this happened definitely at a time when this no longer fell within my competence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just to keep matters simple. Do I understand that it was only after some years that you learned about it for the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Galovic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I just -- Mr. President, just one document I could not show this witness which is necessary, under Rule 90(H). If could I have, Mr. Registrar, a document P1063.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, would it not be fair to the witness to - but correct me when I'm wrong - that it is the position of the Prosecution that it was the talk of town and of common knowledge at the time that such a thing had happened; whereas, the witness testifies that he learned about it only years after that. That's apparently your position, isn't it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I thought in showing the documents and referring to the HTV TV I did that. But let me specifically do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I think the witness has heard what I just said and which you confirmed is the position of the Prosecution. Mr. Galovic, this Chamber has received some evidence about who paid attention at that time to what became known as the Grubori incident, and it's the position of the Prosecution that it was common knowledge, it was talk of the town, it was -- whereas, your testimony is that it was only after a couple of years that you learned about it, and I think, in all fairness, this should be put to you. Any comment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course. I have no comment except to repeat what I have already said, that I learned about it several years later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, do you recognise the document that's on the screen, Mr. Galovic? That's a document issued by your office?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And if you could move to the next page, Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Do you recognise the signature of the person who has signed this document?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is my deputy.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And the seal?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So you identify this document as a document issued by your office?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you. Moving on to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There seems to be some unrest in the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is improper what she's, in our position, Ms. Mahindaratne has not provided [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I don't think this should be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What -- Ms. Mahindaratne, we do not interrupt each other. I have the privilege of interrupting you, but Mr. Misetic was about to tell us why he thought it improper. Can that be done in the presence of the witness, Mr. Misetic, or should it...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In light of the time I will try to be as vague as possible. But I will ask to you look in e-court at Exhibit D918.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is what I wanted to point out: That it should be discussed in the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic says looking at Exhibit D918 would help us out already. So that's the first thing I'll do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I could compare number 1, I think it was improper to ask this witness to authenticate, as Ms. Mahindaratne did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, could you please, in the order you choose, deal with the authenticity of this and/or similar documents in full.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If you could go to page 1 of this document, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Galovic, there is a name in paragraph 1. The name Vunic.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And on top it is written Vunic, Goran. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Does the fact that it's written in hand there render you to question the authenticity of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, at this point, it is incumbent upon Prosecution to show them the document that was received from the Republic of Croatia, which is D918.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I allowed Ms. Mahindaratne, in the order she chooses, to deal with all of it. All the authenticity issues and whether you would start with the one, which apparently what you prefer over the other, that I left in the hands of Ms. Mahindaratne. But I ensured that we'll not just work on the basis of one or -- I take it that you would have done it anyhow if --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Ms. Mahindaratne would have limited herself to one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and the Chamber is not interested in hearing evidence, which is based exclusively on a selective presentation of documents to this witness. But where we start and where we end, that, at this moment, is left in the hands of Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, in the manner that objection was placed before this witness was inappropriate by counsel. I alerted you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let proceed in the next 20 minutes. I noticed that from both sides inappropriateness is invoked. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Do you have -- have -- how do you respond to my question?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. You asked me whether I confirm the authenticity of the signature. Do I confirm the authenticity of the stamp? I do. But not this as well because it was not done in my office. It's out of the question that a document would come from my office corrected by hand. And there's a -- my original document where something else is written. It says Vunic, Boris, and not Vunic, Goran. This document went to the chief of police. No one in the state attorney's office would act in this way, least of all my deputy. So I cannot confirm the authenticity of this. The signature is hers, the stamp is authentic, and the document came from our office but not in this form.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Let me show you the other document, D918, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And if you could go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Galovic, can you look at this document and tell Court if, in fact, this is a document issued by your court -- issued by your office?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judging by the signature, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Is your seal there?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: In the previous document, you identified your seal. And in this document, you don't have a seal. So what is it -- can you explain to the Court as to why -- how this document does not contain a seal whereas the previous document contains a seal?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It can only be attributed to error. That's the only way I can explain it, because it's the same document, the same date. Is it the same date? I'm asking you. Is it the same document with the same date and same contents?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And then I could explain. I -- this document may have come from my office, because a copy remains in the file in the state attorney's office. That copy doesn't have to be stamped. But what is sent out has to be -- bear a seal. But it is the same document.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Moving on to another area, Mr. Galovic. Now, yesterday you testified that -- actually questioned by the Bench about what you seen in Kistanje. You said that you could only remember one house, and last time -- in order to prevent any objections this is what you say: "I'm trying to visualise what I saw at the time, and I'm unable to -- it would be ridiculous to say that I didn't see anything of the sort. Unfortunately, I can't recall that scene in Kistanje, which would leave the impression of total destruction, whereas I can do that in respect of some other places."

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if could I have P203, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: There is, in fact, a document, I appreciate you may not have seen it from the head of security an information service going to the minister of defence. And I'd like to point out, Mr. Galovic, paragraph 4 where it says: "In the liberated area of the hinterlands of Zadar and Sibenik, the establishment of the civilian authorities is not being carried out in a satisfactory pace. More precisely, in the liberated settlements," and there are two places, "Djevrska and Kistanje. The situation is rather chaotic. Incidents of mass burning of houses, plundering of property" -- and there are so many activities being reported. Now this is -- please take note, 8 August 1995. Let me also show you two more documents, and I will ask you the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could have P2349.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: This is, in fact, a report of the Operation Group Sibenik, dated 11 August 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if you could go to page 5 of the English version and page 4 of the Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: There is under item 8, report: "The conduct of the HV members while entering inhabited settlements was correct. However, once the settlements were occupied (particularly places inhabited by Serbs), the commanders lost a -- lost control over their soldiers, which resulted in a number of torched houses and cases of robbery, particularly in the area of Djevrska and Kistanje, and Drnis." And that's dated 11th August.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And if I could have one more document, that's P830. I'm sorry P830 -- or maybe 880. I may have ... If I could just have a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That was correct, P830, Mr. Registrar. It should be a report, not a statement. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, this is a report dated 10th August by the -- reported by monitors from ECMM. And if you could go to page 2 of the English version, as well as the Croatian version. Under the heading, "Humanitarian and human rights matters" the paragraph marked b, it is reported: "Team Knin reported from their patrol today that the villages of Raducic and Rudele were deserted and looted but without any burnt houses. The village of Kistanje, on the other hand, is completely burned and destroyed." This is dated 11th August -- sorry, 10th August. Now, Mr. Galovic, your testimony was that you visited Kistanje twice in the period 10th to 15th August. It seems implausible that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour, the form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it's the technical way in which you put it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. I will rephrase it. I will rephrase, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Trial Chamber as to how it is that such widespread -- such destruction in relation to Kistanje has been reported on the 8th, 10th and 11th, but you, visiting the area between 10th and 15th, twice, saw only one house, or could remember seeing only one burnt house?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that I saw only one house. But I told the Honourable President that I saw at least one. I couldn't say how many. I spoke about my impression. I didn't go to Kistanje, I passed through Kistanje on the way to Knin, and I'm talking about my impression. My impression need not be right, but what I said, and I stand by it, is that I didn't register it. You pass through the main street, the settlement is spread out on both sides of the street. You pass through Kistanje and that is the length of time I was there. There was no reason for me to go to Kistanje, because no one had ever reported to me anything linked to Kistanje, and my job was to go to Knin, to set up a state attorney's office in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And I --

utterances.speaker: IVAN GALOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and that is what I said and that is what I stand by.
